reasoning: Water already at its boiling point turns to steam the instant it meets the burning material, with no sensible heat to absorb first. The change of state carries away a very large latent heat, and the steam produced blankets the fuel and displaces the oxygen feeding the fire. Cold water must first be raised to boiling before any of that happens, and ice must additionally be melted, so both act more slowly even though they absorb more heat in total.
basis: The paper's only disagreement, and the first MED-level split in the corpus — HIGH remains 100% across every paper. Pass A answered boiling water and pass B hot water, and both gave essentially the SAME mechanism (rapid steam formation smothering the fire and carrying off latent heat), so this is a split over degree, not over physics. Adjudicated to boiling water on the SHAPE OF THE OPTION SET: it offers hot water and boiling water as separate alternatives, and every mechanism pass B cites for hot water — lower surface tension, readier vaporisation, steam blanketing — applies MORE strongly to boiling water. An option that is strictly dominated by another option in the same set cannot be the intended key, because the dominating one would be at least as correct. Reading it the other way makes the question defective; reading it as boiling water makes hot water a natural partway distractor and the question sound. The stem's 'more quickly' points the same way: cold water absorbs more heat in total but acts slower, which is the standard trap here.
